results.name: lag1_response_agreement
results.description: Proportion of consecutive rows (same session: trial_index increases by 1) whose yes/no responses agree, minus the agreement expected from the two rows' marginal yes-rate; the model treats responses as independent, so observed above the null means humans perseverate on their previous answer (below: alternate).
results.code:
# name: lag1_response_agreement
# description: Proportion of consecutive rows (same session: trial_index increases by 1) whose yes/no responses agree, minus the agreement expected from the two rows' marginal yes-rate; the model treats responses as independent, so observed above the null means humans perseverate on their previous answer (below: alternate).
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    if len(r) < 3:
        return 0.0
    cons = np.diff(ti) == 1
    if cons.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    a = r[:-1][cons]
    b = r[1:][cons]
    agree = np.mean(a == b)
    p = r.mean()
    return float(agree - (p * p + (1 - p) * (1 - p)))

results.name: target_in_set_yes_rate
results.description: Proportion of "yes" when the target is one of the shown examples; observed below the model's null means the model over-predicts endorsement of already-seen examples (humans lapse/hedge even on members), above means it under-predicts it.

results.name: near_minus_far_gradient
results.description: Yes-rate for non-example targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets more than 40 away; observed below the null means the model's generalisation gradient over numerical distance is too steep (humans are flatter), above means too shallow.
results.code:
# name: near_minus_far_gradient
# description: Yes-rate for non-example targets within 3 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets more than 40 away; observed below the null means the model's generalisation gradient over numerical distance is too steep (humans are flatter), above means too shallow.
def test_statistic(df):
    arr = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values[:, None]
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(arr - t), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    near = (dist > 0) & (dist <= 3)
    far = dist > 40
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share a parity, and non-example targets, yes-rate when the target shares that parity minus when it does not; observed below the null means the model over-weights parity (even/odd rules) relative to humans, above means it under-weights it.
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share a parity, and non-example targets, yes-rate when the target shares that parity minus when it does not; observed below the null means the model over-weights parity (even/odd rules) relative to humans, above means it under-weights it.
def test_statistic(df):
    arr = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(arr), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    par = np.mod(arr, 2)
    mx = np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(par, axis=1)
    same = (mx == mn) & (n >= 2)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(arr - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    keep = same & (dist > 0)
    match = np.mod(t, 2) == mx
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = keep & match
    b = keep & ~match
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: trial_index_drift
results.description: Yes-rate in the first half of the session (trial_index below median) minus yes-rate in the second half; the model has no time dependence, so observed above the null means humans become more conservative over the session in a way the model does not produce (below: more liberal).
results.code:
# name: trial_index_drift
# description: Yes-rate in the first half of the session (trial_index below median) minus yes-rate in the second half; the model has no time dependence, so observed above the null means humans become more conservative over the session in a way the model does not produce (below: more liberal).
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].values.astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    med = np.median(ti)
    early = ti < med
    late = ti >= med
    if early.sum() == 0 or late.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[early].mean() - r[late].mean())

results.name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation, across example sets with at least 20 responses, of the per-set yes-rate; observed above the null means the model makes sets too similar in overall generality (under-produces set-to-set differences in concept breadth), below means it exaggerates them.

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Proportion of "yes" for targets more than 40 away from every example; observed above the model's null means the model under-produces broad/random endorsement of distant targets (e.g. missing lapse or very broad concepts), below means it over-produces it.

results.name: recency_order_effect
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples and non-example targets, yes-rate when the target is strictly closer to the last-shown example than to the first-shown one minus the reverse; the model is order-invariant, so observed above the null means humans show recency (weight the last example more), below means primacy.
results.code:
# name: recency_order_effect
# description: For sets of 2+ examples and non-example targets, yes-rate when the target is strictly closer to the last-shown example than to the first-shown one minus the reverse; the model is order-invariant, so observed above the null means humans show recency (weight the last example more), below means primacy.
def test_statistic(df):
    arr = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(arr), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    first = arr[:, 0]
    idx = np.clip(n - 1, 0, arr.shape[1] - 1)
    last = arr[np.arange(len(arr)), idx]
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(arr - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    df_ = np.abs(first - t)
    dl = np.abs(last - t)
    ok = (n >= 2) & (dmin > 0)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = ok & (dl < df_)
    b = ok & (df_ < dl)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
